The authors fabricated six types of surfaces: hydrophilic, hydrophobic, superhydrophilic (SHPi), superhydrophobic (SHPo), biphilic, and superbiphilic.
SHPi surfaces nucleated at a surface superheat about 3 times lower than hydrophilic surfaces.
Hydrophobic surfaces nucleated at superheats about 10 times lower than hydrophilic surfaces, and SHPo surfaces nucleated at superheats another order of magnitude lower than hydrophobic surfaces.
The maximum heat transfer coefficient (HTC) of the biphilic surface was 2-4 times larger than the HTC of the hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces, respectively.
Biphilic surfaces with 50 μm hydrophobic spots had higher HTCs at high superheat compared to surfaces with 400 μm spots.
Superbiphilic surfaces achieved critical heat fluxes over 100 W/cm^2 and heat transfer coefficients over 100 kW/m^2K.
The authors developed an analytical model to describe how the wettability and topography of biphilic surfaces affect boiling heat transfer.
Nucleation measurements showed that SHPo surfaces nucleated at superheat temperatures significantly lower than the typical thermocouple measurement uncertainty of ±1.5 K.
The authors found that the wettability that optimizes HTC is a function of the superheat at which the surface operates.
The random nature of the nanostructuring process used to create SHPi surfaces led to significant measurement noise in the HTC data.
The authors assumed that the wetting line of the bubble on a biphilic surface advances until pinning occurs at the edge of the hydrophobic spot.
The number of active nucleation sites on the hydrophobic regions of a biphilic surface cannot exceed the number of hydrophobic spots.
The modeling results underpredicted the very high HTC values obtained on SHPi surfaces, likely due to additional wicking effects not captured by the model.
The agreement between the model and experiments was better at low superheat (T<15K) than at larger superheat (T>15K) for biphilic surfaces, probably because the modeling neglected shear forces.
The authors were not able to manufacture surfaces with 3° wetting angles on the hydrophilic regions, so only modeling results were shown for that case.
